name: Landmarks around Great Bookham
method: Massing models fitted to whatever footprint OpenStreetMap holds. Polesden Lacey, St Barnabas Ranmore and St Nicolas Great Bookham are rebuilt from published descriptions of the buildings — chiefly listed-building entries — and cite them in a sources field. The rest are still written from the model's own knowledge and say so in their confidence field. No photographs were used: this tool reads text, not images, and a listing describes form and material more precisely than a photograph would anyway.
confidence_scale: high = I am confident this building has this form. medium = the form is typical of the building type and I believe it applies here. low = plausible massing, treat as a placeholder.

models.name: Polesden Lacey
models.confidence: high — rebuilt from the Grade II* list entry, not from memory
sources: Historic England list entry 1028665 (Grade II*), via search: 'The two-storey house is stuccoed, and is in the form of a quadrangle around a large central courtyard with an apsidal end'; 'stucco on brick, slate roofs, and stuccoed chimneys'; 'two storeys, with a prominent cornice carried round'; 'windows are mainly 12-pane sashes'.
Same entry on the cupola: 'In the centre of the roof is a tall octagonal 2-stage cupola with windows in the lower stage, clock-faces in the upper, a prominent cornice, and domed roof with finial.'

Same entry on the east front: 'The symmetrical east front is E-plan ... 3:3:3 bays between projecting wings, and has a projecting pedimented centre ... a semi-circular bow front to the right hand wing by Mewes and Davis.'
Build history: 1821-24 by Thomas Cubitt for Joseph Bonsor; extended 1902-6 by Sir Ambrose Poynter for William McEwan; enlarged 1906-9 for Ronald Greville by Mewes and Davis.
models.note: Rebuilt from the listed-building description rather than from memory. The quadrangle around a central courtyard is confirmed, and so is the thing I had guessed at and flagged: there IS a clock feature, but it is a tall OCTAGONAL two-stage cupola with a domed roof and finial, not the square turret I invented. The grand front is the EAST front, E-plan, with projecting wings, a pedimented centre, and a semi-circular bow on one wing — which is why this model is placed by compass rather than by whichever edge of the polygon is longest. Chimneys are stuccoed, not brick.

parts.note: E-plan: north projecting wing of the east front
E-plan: south projecting wing of the east front
the semi-circular bow front Mewes and Davis added to the right-hand wing
the projecting pedimented centre of the east front (Ionic doorcase below)
cupola, upper stage — clock faces, cornice, domed roof with finial

models.name: St Nicolas Church, Great Bookham
models.confidence: high — checked against the parish's own building history
models.note: Saxon nave, Norman tower stonework, and a 14th-century WOODEN tower stage carrying the shingled spire — which is the thing you see across the village. Modelled in three stages accordingly: stone below, timber above, shingles on top. There is also a 1380 south porch with a priest's room over it, modelled as the small block on the south side.

parts.note: Saxon nave and 1341 chancel, stone and flint
south porch of 1380 with the priest's room above it

sources: Grade I listed. Nave built 1042-1080 (two Saxon windows survive high on the north side); Normans extended the nave and added the tower stonework in the 12th century; 'a wooden tower and shingle covered spire was built in the 14th-century'; large chancel 1341; south porch 1380 with a priest's room above. Stone and flint.

models.name: St Barnabas Church, Ranmore Common
models.confidence: high — checked against descriptions of the building
models.note: Gilbert Scott's 'High Victoriana' estate church for the Cubitts of Denbies, Early English Gothic Revival. Two things the sources corrected: the exterior is rounded FLINT COBBLE, not ashlar stone, and the spire does not sit straight on the tower — it rises off an OCTAGONAL stage, which is modelled here as an octagon between the two.

parts.note: the octagon the spire stands on
the tall slender spire seen from every hill in Surrey

sources: Sir George Gilbert Scott, consecrated 1859, for George Cubitt of Denbies. 'The exterior is entirely faced in rounded flint cobbles'; 'a prominent spire on an octagon'; the tall slender spire stands 700 ft above sea level and is seen from hills across Surrey.

models.name: St Mary's Church, Fetcham
models.note: Parish church with Saxon and Norman fabric, flint walls, a squat west tower. Modelled as a typical Surrey village church: low nave, embattled tower, no spire.

models.name: St Michael's Church, Mickleham
models.note: Norman church in the Mole valley, flint with a west tower and a short pyramidal cap rather than a spire.

models.name: The Old Barn Hall, Great Bookham
models.note: A converted barn serving as the village hall, on Church Road. Modelled as what it is: one long single-volume space under a steep continuous gabled roof, eaves low to the ground.

models.name: Norbury Park House
models.note: Georgian villa on the slope above the Mole, in the estate woodland. Modelled as a compact three-storey block with a low hipped roof — the standard form for a house of that date and size. Detail is a placeholder.

models.name: Juniper Hall, Mickleham
models.note: Georgian house at the foot of Box Hill, now a field studies centre. Three storeys, rendered, low hipped roof. Placeholder massing.

models.name: Bookham station
models.confidence: medium on scale, low on detail
models.note: A Mole Valley line halt: low single-storey buildings on the platforms, not a trainshed. Modelled low deliberately — the estimator's instinct is to make anything tagged train_station 14 m tall, which is wrong for a village halt.

models.name: Effingham Junction station
models.confidence: medium on scale, low on detail
models.note: Junction station with a depot alongside. Same reasoning as Bookham: low platform buildings, not a terminus.

known_gaps: These are massing models, not architecture. A church gets a nave, a tower and a spire of about the right height; it does not get its aisles, porch, transepts or windows.
Nothing here is measured. Heights are judged from the building type and from how these places read in the landscape, not from drawings.

A model only applies if OpenStreetMap has the building mapped AND named close to the way this file spells it. Where OSM has no footprint, nothing is drawn — deliberately, so a wrong guess can never put a building in an empty field.
Coordinates are approximate. They exist only to stop 'St Mary's Church' matching the wrong St Mary's; the radius is generous for that reason.
Polesden Lacey is modelled range by range because it is a courtyard house; the others are massing in two or three volumes. All of them are still proportion and silhouette, not architecture.
sources_caveat: The network proxy in the build environment blocks historicengland.org.uk, wikipedia.org and nationaltrust.org.uk directly, so the quotations recorded above came back through web search results quoting those pages rather than from reading the pages first-hand. They read as verbatim listing text and are consistent across sources, but they have not been checked against the primary entry. No photographs were used at any point: this tool reads text, not images.
